title: WPF and WinForms
sub: Who checks the thread, how await returns via Post, Invoke, Progress<T> and Task.Run
cards/0/body:
Why can't you touch a control from another thread? A Windows window belongs to the thread that created it: its messages arrive only in that thread's queue. And the internal structures of WPF elements (the tree, layout, bindings) aren't protected by locks: they're designed for a single thread.

WPF. Every element derives from DispatcherObject. On creation it remembers the current thread's Dispatcher, the object that manages that thread's queue. Reading and writing properties (Text, Content, Value...) starts with a VerifyAccess() check. Wrong thread: InvalidOperationException: The calling thread cannot access this object because a different thread owns it. The check always runs, in Debug and in Release. To check without an exception, call CheckAccess(): it returns false.

WinForms. The check sits in access to the window handle (Control.Handle), which almost every property goes through: InvalidOperationException: Cross-thread operation not valid: Control 'label1' accessed from a thread other than the thread it was created on. But it's switched on by the Control.CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls flag, which defaults to true only under a debugger. In a Release build without a debugger a cross-thread access may "work" and break the window later, at a random moment.
cards/1/q: A WPF button handler does await Task.Run(() => progressBar.Value = 50). What happens?
cards/1/options/0: InvalidOperationException: the lambda runs on a pool thread, and the ProgressBar belongs to the UI thread
cards/1/options/1: It works: Task.Run was called from the UI thread, so the lambda runs there
cards/1/options/2: The exception only happens under a debugger; in Release the code works
cards/1/explain: Task.Run always hands the lambda to the pool. VerifyAccess in the Value setter sees a foreign thread and throws, in any WPF build. "Only under a debugger" is about WinForms.
cards/2/q: WinForms, a Release build running without a debugger. A System.Threading.Timer callback (it runs on a pool thread) writes label1.Text. What's most likely?
cards/2/options/0: There may be no exception: the check is on by default only under a debugger, and the window may break later
cards/2/options/2: A compile error: a control can't be accessed from a timer lambda
cards/2/explain: CheckForIllegalCrossThreadCalls defaults to true only when a debugger is attached. No exception doesn't mean the code is correct.
cards/3/title: How await gets back to the UI: Post and Send
cards/3/body:
From u4.l1: at the pause, await captures SynchronizationContext.Current and later calls its Post. A context has two main methods:

  • Post(callback): queue it to the target thread and return immediately;
  • Send(callback): run it on the target thread and wait until it finishes.

await only uses Post: the thread that completed the task has no reason to stand and wait for the UI thread.

In WPF the UI thread's context is DispatcherSynchronizationContext: its Post calls Dispatcher.BeginInvoke, and Send calls Dispatcher.Invoke. In WinForms it's WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext: Post calls Control.BeginInvoke, Send calls Control.Invoke. Both BeginInvokes do the same thing: put the delegate into the UI thread's queue, and the message loop runs it when it gets there.
cards/3/deep: DispatcherSynchronizationContext's Post queues the delegate at the Dispatcher's normal priority, which is higher than input and rendering. So a steady stream of short continuations (hundreds of Posts per second) can delay painting the window even though each piece is fast.
cards/4/task: After await the handler writes label.Text. Someone added ConfigureAwait(false), and everything broke. Fix it: the continuation must come back through Post into the UI thread's queue.
cards/5/title: Getting back to the UI thread by hand: Invoke and BeginInvoke
cards/5/body:
await brings you back to the UI on its own. But sometimes you're already on another thread with no await in sight: a System.Threading.Timer callback, a third-party library event, a FileSystemWatcher. Then you call the Dispatcher or the control directly. These are the same calls that sit inside Post and Send:

  • Dispatcher.Invoke / Control.Invoke: run on the UI thread and wait until it's done;
  • Dispatcher.BeginInvoke / Control.BeginInvoke: queue it and return immediately;
  • Dispatcher.InvokeAsync: like BeginInvoke, but returns an operation you can await.

In WinForms InvokeRequired returns true when you're not on the UI thread. On .NET Framework a lambda for Invoke/BeginInvoke must be cast to a delegate explicitly (new Action(…)); newer WinForms versions on .NET have overloads that take an Action.

The Invoke trap is the same cycle as in u4.l2, just assembled by hand: 1) the UI thread is blocked on .Wait() of a background task; 2) the background calls Dispatcher.Invoke and waits for the UI thread; 3) the UI thread isn't draining its queue: deadlock. BeginInvoke and InvokeAsync don't wait, so they don't close that cycle.
cards/6/q: WPF. After a click the window hangs forever. Why?
cards/6/options/0: Dispatcher.Invoke waits for the UI thread to run the delegate, but the UI thread is blocked on t.Wait() and isn't draining its queue
cards/6/options/1: The Task.Run lambda runs on the UI thread, which is busy with t.Wait()
cards/6/options/2: Dispatcher.Invoke can't be called from a pool thread: it throws, and the task never completes
cards/6/explain: The background waits for the UI thread, the UI thread waits for the background. With Dispatcher.InvokeAsync there'd be no cycle, but the window would still freeze on Wait(). The real fix is await t instead of t.Wait().
cards/7/body:
Background work often needs to report how it's going: "37%". You could call the Dispatcher straight from the computation, but then the computation knows about the window. The idiomatic way is the IProgress<T> interface with a single Report(T value) method, and its implementation Progress<T>:

  • 1. The Progress<T> constructor remembers SynchronizationContext.Current of the thread where it was created. Created in a handler, it remembers the UI thread's context.
  • 2. The background calls Report(i). Progress Posts to the remembered context and returns immediately: the computation doesn't wait for the UI.
  • 3. The UI thread takes the delegate from its queue and runs your callback: you can touch controls there.

Consequences. The callback arrives later than Report, so don't pass a mutable object: it may change before the callback runs. And if Progress is created where there's no context (inside Task.Run, in a console app), the callbacks go to the thread pool.
cards/8/q: WPF. Progress was created inside Task.Run. What happens when Import calls Report?
cards/8/options/0: The callback runs on a pool thread and fails with InvalidOperationException on bar.Value
cards/8/options/1: It works: Progress<T> always runs the callback on the UI thread
cards/8/options/2: Report blocks the pool thread until the UI thread runs the callback
cards/8/explain: Progress remembers the context in its constructor, and on a pool thread SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so the callbacks go to the pool. Create Progress in the handler, before Task.Run.
cards/9/title: Where the window freezes: before await and after await
cards/9/body:
await by itself doesn't move work off the UI thread. The window freezes in two places:

  • 1. Before the first await. Until its first pause an async method works like an ordinary one (u2.l1): on the calling thread, that is, the UI thread.
  • 2. After await. The continuation came back to the UI thread through Post, and everything that follows runs there too. A heavy computation after awaiting a download freezes the window just as it would without any async.

The fix: hand the heavy part to the pool with Task.Run and show the result after await. If the method doesn't touch the UI itself (a computation in a library), you can put ConfigureAwait(false) on its await: then the pool runs the continuation along with the computation.
cards/10/q: WPF. After a click the window freezes for 3 seconds. Why?
cards/10/options/0: HeavyCompute runs after await: the continuation came back to the UI thread
cards/10/options/1: LoadAsync blocks the UI thread while it downloads
cards/10/options/2: The await in Calc_Click holds the UI thread until CalculateAsync completes
cards/10/explain: await LoadAsync captured the DispatcherSynchronizationContext, and the HeavyCompute line ran on the UI thread. The fix: await Task.Run(() => HeavyCompute(data)), or ConfigureAwait(false) on await LoadAsync, since CalculateAsync doesn't touch the UI.
cards/11/q: The handler does await SaveReportAsync(), and the window freezes for 3 s right after the click. There's a ConfigureAwait(false), so why?
cards/11/options/0: RenderPdf runs synchronously before the first await, on the UI thread; ConfigureAwait(false) only affects code after a pause
cards/11/options/1: ConfigureAwait(false) sent the continuation back to the UI thread
cards/11/options/2: File.WriteAllBytesAsync holds the UI thread until the write finishes
cards/11/explain: Before the first await the method is plain synchronous code on the calling thread. To leave the UI thread before the computation you need Task.Run: var pdf = await Task.Run(() => RenderPdf(report));
cards/12/q: A WPF handler: var mesh = await Task.Run(() => BuildMesh(points)); viewport.Show(mesh). Put what happens after the click in order
cards/12/items/0: The handler starts on the UI thread
cards/12/items/1: Task.Run queues the computation to the pool, await returns control
cards/12/items/2: The UI thread is free and handles clicks
cards/12/items/3: The computation finishes; Post sends the continuation into the UI thread's queue
cards/12/items/4: The UI thread runs the code after await and shows the result
cards/12/explain: While the pool computes, the window stays alive: the UI thread drains the queue that the continuation will later arrive in.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: WPF: run on the UI thread and wait
cards/13/pairs/1/1: WinForms: queue to the UI thread
cards/13/pairs/2/1: Report Posts to the context where it was created
cards/13/pairs/4/1: Throws if the thread isn't the owner
